title: The early church, looking back
tomorrow: a window made of broken pieces. why does it glow?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel's story: walls down, exile, and a temple rebuilt to weeping and shouting. Still faithful. Today, the people who came next.

Saying what you actually believe can cost a little: a comment, an unfollow, a weird look at lunch. In Acts it costs Stephen everything. Stones are flying, and he says two things out loud. “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And then, kneeling: “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” Nearby, the crowd's coats lie at the feet of a young man named Saul. So, one question for today: what's worth saying out loud?
screen: `A COMMENT, AN UNFOLLOW.` → `STEPHEN, UNDER THE STONES.` → `WHAT'S WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD?`

segments.voice: The early church answers with one word from Acts. Jesus tells his friends, “ye shall be witnesses unto me.” Looking back, they witnessed three ways. With a life laid down: Stephen, and others tradition remembers, like Perpetua, a young mother in North Africa, and Polycarp, a bishop who would not curse Christ. With a life given away: tradition says a young Egyptian named Antony heard a Gospel line read in church, “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor,” did it, and went into the desert to pray. And with a voice joined to other voices: the creeds, short statements of faith meant to be said together. Now a neighbor who says it out loud too. When a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first, Jesus answers with Israel's own words, the Shema, from Deuteronomy. In the Jewish Publication Society's translation: “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.” Deuteronomy says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up, and Jewish prayer keeps them evening and morning. Shared ground: a short line about who God is, said aloud, sometimes at great cost. And one honest difference. The Christian creeds go on to confess God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Jews hear the Shema's oneness without a Trinity. Two peoples, each saying it in their own words.
screen: `YE SHALL BE WITNESSES.` · `A LIFE LAID DOWN, A LIFE GIVEN AWAY.` · `A NEIGHBOR: HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `ONE GOD, SAID TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `THE FIRST WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Stand up, the way some congregations stand to say what they believe together. Say one early name quietly, Stephen, Perpetua, Polycarp or Antony, or a saint your own church remembers, and stay standing for a few breaths with the one thing they did that you'd want to carry. Then sit for the bell; if you pray, give thanks for them.
The early church. Martyrs, monks and creeds: people who told what they had seen, with their lives and with their voices.
The line to keep: the first witnesses, and the young man holding the coats becomes one of them. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Churches that keep a calendar of saints remember Stephen, Perpetua, Polycarp and Antony on their feast days, and some congregations say the Nicene Creed together at Sunday worship; Jews say the Shema in evening and morning prayer.

fork.setup: your little sister asks why people at church say the creed together, instead of each saying what they personally believe. what does the early church suggest?
options: it's only an old habit, with no real reason behind it.
a creed is witness said with other voices, carrying each other.
it's so nobody can tell who doesn't believe it.
fork.reveal: the creeds were made to be said together, out loud: one of three ways the early church witnessed, beside lives laid down and lives given away.

options: Alike and different: both say who God is out loud. Our creeds add Father, Son and Spirit.

chat.meaning: Jesus himself answers with the Shema (Mark 12:29). Shared: a line about God said aloud. Different: creeds confess the Trinity; Jews hear God's oneness without it.

Polycarp.meaning: an early bishop who would not curse Christ

Antony.meaning: an Egyptian who gave everything away and prayed in the desert

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: wisdom). Title, word and carry kept; Acts 1:8, 7:59–60, Matthew 19:21 and the early writings kept. The unity thread (the Shema) is new.

Unity thread: shared = a short line about who God is, said aloud (Jesus answers the scribe with the Shema, Mark 12:29, quoting Deuteronomy 6:4). Neighbor's own words from the JPS 1917 translation: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' Honest difference = the Christian creeds confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit; Jews hear God's oneness without a Trinity. No ranking. A Jewish reader should confirm the wording and that 'Jewish prayer keeps them evening and morning' (from Deuteronomy 6:7) is fair.
Hard scene: Stephen's stoning (Acts 7) is told in one line without detail. For parents: the hook names stones flying; nothing graphic follows.

Antony: Athanasius' Life of Antony says he heard Matthew 19:21 read in church and acted on it; framed as 'tradition says'. Perpetua as a young mother in North Africa and Polycarp refusing to curse Christ come from their martyr accounts, framed as 'tradition remembers'. No ages or dates.
'Some congregations stand to say what they believe together' (the practice) is a soft claim; confirm.
Deliberately not claimed: that the English word 'martyr' comes from Greek martys. The original game only says Acts 1:8 uses the word for witnesses.
